general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: ARVC is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes in some European registries, but it can present in the sixth decade
Myoclonic jerks are common during syncope and are a frequent reason for a misdiagnosis of epilepsy
The 2010 Task Force Criteria use major and minor criteria in six categories: RV structure and function, tissue characterisation, repolarisation, depolarisation, arrhythmias and family history
Avoidance of high-intensity exercise is recommended in ARVC because exercise accelerates disease progression and raises arrhythmic risk
First-degree relatives of ARVC patients are screened with ECG, echocardiography and cardiac MRI even when asymptomatic

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Williams is a 55-year-old physically active man and high school basketball coach who presents to the emergency department after being transferred from an outside community hospital where he was evaluated for two episodes of loss of consciousness with witnessed 'shaking.' He was playing in a recreational basketball game approximately three hours ago when, during an intense sprint down the court, he suddenly collapsed forward without warning. Multiple witnesses, including fellow coaches, describe him falling to the ground and becoming rigid for 2-3 seconds followed by approximately 10-15 seconds of bilateral upper and lower extremity jerking movements. He was unresponsive during the episode. Upon regaining consciousness approximately 30 seconds after collapse, he appeared briefly dazed for about 30-60 seconds but then rapidly returned to baseline, asking 'what happened?' and wanting to get back into the game. He denied any chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath preceding the event. He reports no aura, no unusual taste or smell, and no preceding deja vu. Against advice, he rested on the bench for 15 minutes and then attempted to re-enter the game. During a fast break approximately 20 minutes later, he collapsed again with similar witnessed jerking lasting roughly 10 seconds. EMS was called and he was taken to the outside hospital where an ECG was obtained showing normal sinus rhythm at 76 bpm with no significant abnormalities. A CT head without contrast was unremarkable. He was loaded with levetiracetam 1000 mg IV and transferred here with a diagnosis of 'new-onset seizures, likely exercise-induced epilepsy.' His wife, who arrived at the outside hospital, reports that he has never had a seizure before but mentions that approximately six weeks ago he had a 'near-blackout' while running up the stairs at school carrying equipment, which he attributed to dehydration. She is visibly distressed and mentions that his father 'dropped dead' at age 49 while jogging. A repeat 12-lead ECG has been requested. He is currently asymptomatic and appears well.
